items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' at the open. He does signpost mid-call — 'let me run you through the way that our pricing works' — but the customer never got a roadmap or a time expectation up front, and there was no confirmation ask anywhere in the call.

Neither address was collected. Not the origin, not the destination, not a zip, not even a city. Jack then budgeted 'two to three hours to get to drive and get everything unloaded' on a distance he had no information about, and quoted a $3,380 total built partly on that guess. He also never mentioned a trip fee, which he cannot rule out without knowing where the new house is. On a two-day, twelve-hour job this is the largest single unknown in the quote and it was never asked.
Storage stops and additional stops never asked.

Access concerns never probed at either end — no parking, no driveway, no HOA, no question about whether the new house is a townhome too or whether the crew can back a truck up to it. For a three-story townhome origin, the loading situation is a material variable.

The moving-stressor question was never asked. The customer did volunteer flexibility and uncertainty — 'our closing date might have shifted a bit' — and Jack treated it purely as a scheduling fact rather than an opening.

The what's-included list was partial: 'our typical moving service is all inclusive. We wrap everything, disassemble reassemble pretty much absolutely everything.' Gas, truck, taxes and insurance were never named, and the full no-hidden-fees pitch (no credit card fees, no transportation fee, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees) was replaced by the narrower 'there's no deposits and there's no cancellation or rescheduling fees.'
Trip fee never addressed. With no destination on file he had no basis to say whether one applies, and the customer will find out from the confirmation email or from the bill.

No Worries Damage Coverage was explained genuinely well but never named. 'We include a lot of damage coverage, we include up to $2,000 for every single move and that's value based coverage. So a lot of companies just do based on weight and then it's like a whole insurance debacle... we'd pay the whole value of that item' is the right substance, but the customer never heard the brand name and cannot repeat it to her husband, who is the second decision maker on this call.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.
No sense-check anywhere. The pricing, clock, packing-materials and estimate content ran as one long block, and the customer's side across it is 'Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Oh, okay.'

Truck count never stated. Mover counts were given precisely for both days (two on the pack day, three on the move day) but the customer does not know whether a three-story townhome plus a full pack fits in one truck or two.
Walk distance never asked at either end, on a three-story townhome where the carry from the third floor to the curb is the whole job.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used — no school-bus reference or similar to make twelve hours across two days feel concrete before the $3,380 number landed.

The Save Your Ass speech is present in fragments but never delivered. Jack made the prep-equals-money link twice and correctly — on the TV mounts, 'if you do it, obviously we get there and it's less time for us so it's less money for you all,' and on staging, 'if there's anything you are comfortable with us wrapping or prepping then that'll just help us make the move day go even faster.' Both are real. What never came is the consolidation list (kids' toys, loose items in drawers, garden tools, photos off the walls), the take-a-carload tip, or a 'does that make sense?' close. On a full-pack job the carload tip is less relevant, but the consolidation speech is more relevant, not less — every loose item the crew has to box is billable packing time, and the customer said twice that the house is minimalist, which means she is exactly the person who would act on the instruction.

Booking attempt was soft and conditional. 'If you guys do decide to move forward there's no deposits and there's no cancellation or rescheduling fees. If you ever just want to pick a date and hold it there's no payments upfront so if ever have a date and we'll lock it in, we can hold it for you.' Every clause is hypothetical. She had already said 'I will relay this to my husband' and 'we've got a little bit of flex time' — the ask that was sitting there is 'want me to hold the seventeenth while you two talk?' and it never came.

No bolded-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections' — a real cost on this call specifically, because the entire quote is going to be re-explained secondhand by the customer to her husband Wesley, and the only artifact he will see is the email.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' The customer raised two of her own (TV mounts, curtain rods) and both were answered well, but he never opened the door himself before closing.
No hours and no how-to-reach-us. She has no callback number, no name to ask for beyond 'Jack,' and no idea when the office is open.
Customer's name used once — 'hey Rachel, this is Jack with Einstein' at the open, and never again across ten minutes.
top_strength: Jack's discovery on the packing scope is the best probing in this week's sample and it is worth playing for the team. Rather than accepting 'help with packing' at face value off the web form, he opened by disambiguating it: 'First thing I saw you put help with packing. Were you needing us to come in and box up just everything in the house or were you referring to like wrapping?' Then, having established a full pack, he went after the two variables that actually drive packing hours instead of asking generic questions. On the kitchen: 'packing is one of the harder things to gauge over the phone. Decor, fragile and glassware obviously takes more time than anything, the kitchen. Would you describe the kitchen as every cabinet, every shelf full of glassware or a bit more minimal?' Then the same question for the rest of the house: 'kind of same thing about like decor around the house. Lots of shelves and knick-knacks or minimal?' And then the one that carries real dollars: 'most of our boxes are all pretty cheap, wardrobes are the one cost, they're like $18 each, they can kind of add up a little bit. Is there a lot of hanging clothes that need to be boxed up in wardrobes?' — which got him a sized answer ('probably two walk-in closets, seven feet by four feet with two racks on each side'). He also told the truth about the uncertainty instead of hiding it: 'packing quoting could be, you could go to a house and it could be a multiple days deal or it could be super easy. So you never know.' That is how a rep earns the right to give a range. His crew sizing was reasoned out loud rather than asserted, with the customer's interest built in: 'I think we'll probably need three movers with all of the stairs and everything. I think it's just gonna make everything easier and faster and safer. But with packing, we could probably just do the two movers,' and then the giveback — 'if for some reason we are able to pack prep and get everything super nice and ready on day one we might be like, hey, we don't need a third mover, we can do this for two and we can get rid of them.' Rate framing was the cleanest in the sample: per mover, per hour, with day-of-week tiers stated unprompted and the arithmetic done for her — '$106 per mover on the weekends, Fridays and Saturdays, and then it's $101 per mover on weekdays.' The damage-coverage explanation was substantively excellent — value-based versus weight-based, with the contrast named — and it produced the best moment on the call: she heard 'TV' and immediately asked a question she had been sitting on, 'I'm assuming that we need to take TVs off of their mount,' which opened into curtain rods and a genuinely useful answer ('we'll take the TV off the mount, we'll wrap up the TV, we'll take the TV mount down. We just can't remount anything at the new place'). She closed with 'Thank you so much for walking through all of that with me,' which is the right verdict on the discovery work.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: get the addresses, every call, before the pricing block. Jack quoted a $3,380 two-day job without ever asking where the new house is. He then priced 'two to three hours to get to drive and get everything unloaded' into the estimate, which means a meaningful chunk of a twelve-hour quote is resting on an unstated assumption about a distance he never confirmed, and he has no way to know whether a trip fee applies. Everything else on this call was well-reasoned; this is the one input that makes the whole number unfalsifiable. Second priority, and it is the one that likely costs the booking: this was a two-decision-maker call and Jack sold to one of them. Rachel said 'I will relay this to my husband' and closed with 'I'll talk to Wesley about it and try to get something loosely nailed down once we know the moving date.' Everything Jack built in ten minutes — the crew logic, the materials transparency, the value-based coverage argument — now has to survive being repeated secondhand by someone who heard it once. The move is to put the hold and the email to work on Wesley's behalf: 'Totally get it. Two things that'll make that conversation easier — first, there's no deposit and no cancellation fee, so I can hold the seventeenth right now and you lose nothing if you two decide differently. Second, I'm putting the numbers at the top of this email in bold so Wesley can read them himself rather than getting my version through you — the pack-day rate, the move-day rate, the materials, and the total. Reply to it with any corrections if I've got the details wrong.' That single move converts a soft 'if you ever want to pick a date' into a held date, delivers the email-verification handoff he skipped, and puts the quote in front of the actual second decision maker. Third, name the differentiators. Jack explained No Worries Damage Coverage better than almost anyone in this sample and never said its name, which means Rachel cannot repeat it. Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee never came up at all, and both are cheap adds on a job where the crew is in the customer's house for two consecutive days. Estimate-accuracy note, and this one is comparatively clean: the twelve-hour, two-day structure for a three-story townhome with a full pack is defensible, he showed his work ('about three hours to get everything loaded and then two to three hours to drive and get everything unloaded'), and he did not pad — he explicitly built in the possibility of dropping the third mover and said 'you only pay for the actual materials used.' The one soft spot is the unbounded drive assumption noted above. Worth pulling the actual if it books, specifically to see whether packing a minimalist three-bedroom townhome really runs five to six hours; that is the number most likely to move, and the honest uncertainty Jack named out loud is exactly the kind of variance the bottom-four review is trying to convert into a rule of thumb. One small add: the customer is buying $18 wardrobe boxes and packing materials — that is a live Ecobox referral and it went unmade.
phone_presence_notes: Easy, natural energy throughout — 'Cool,' 'Awesome,' 'Of course,' 'Yeah, we try to make it easy' — and he built enough comfort that the customer volunteered two questions of her own about TV mounts and curtain rods and thanked him unprompted for 'walking through all of that with me'; held at 4 rather than 5 by using her name exactly once and letting a long uninterrupted pricing and estimate block reduce her to a run of 'Mm-hmm' before the total landed.
